main.text: [III, 305] [col. 472] Chapter 5.
What Joel has about the locusts in chapter two.

In the prophecy of Joel, ch. II, 1. and 2., we read: Let all the inhabitants of the [col. 473] land tremble: for the day of the Lord is coming; for it is near. A day of darkness and gloom; a day of cloud and obscurity; like the dawn spread upon the mountains: a people great and strong. The like of it has never been from of old, nor shall be again after it, to the years of every generation.] As he earlier called the locusts a strong and innumerable nation, so here he calls them a great and strong people: this metaphor has already been explained. He denies that a people like them either has been or will be, as above in ch. I, 2. The time at which they will come is called the day of the Lord, because the Lord will then summon the guilty to trial and exact punishment from them. And it is a day of darkness and gloom, because in Scripture, just as light denotes prosperity, so darkness denotes adversity. And it is compared with the dawn spread upon the mountains, to signify that this evil will spread both widely and swiftly. For both are proper to the dawn, whose light is scattered everywhere in an instant. In the same sense Isaiah LVIII, 8. said: Your light shall break forth like the dawn. That is, οἷον ἀςραπῆς τινος δίκην, σὺν ὁρμῇ καὶ δρόμῳ καθιέμενον παρὰ Θεοῦ [hoion astrapēs tinos dikēn, syn hormē kai dromō kathiemenon para Theou], sent forth by God with force and speed like lightning, as Cyril has it there. Moreover, the poets too speak of the dawn being spread or scattered. Homer, at the beginning of Iliad ϑ' [8],
Ἠὼς μὲν κροκόπεπλος ἐκίδνατο πᾶσαν ἐπ' αἶαν. [Ēōs men krokopeplos ekidnato pasan ep' aian.]
Which Virgil rendered thus in book 4 of the Aeneid:
And now early Dawn, leaving the saffron couch of Tithonus, was scattering fresh light upon the earth.
And in book 12 of the Aeneid:
The next day was scarcely scattering the mountain-tops with light.
Here we read of scattering the mountains with its light, as in the Prophet, Like the dawn spread upon the mountains: because light appears first on the mountains ^{R1}.

[III, 306] Verse 3. Before it fire shall consume, and behind it a flame shall burn. The land was like the garden of Eden before it; but behind it shall be a vast desert; nor shall anything escape it.] Some hold that the locusts themselves are compared here, and above in ch. I, 19. 20., with fire and flame, because, on the authority of Pliny ^{a)}, they scorch many things by their touch. Hence in the life of Aphraates the monk, Theodoret describes locusts as πυρὶ παραπλησίως ἅπαντα προσδαπανώσας [pyri paraplēsiōs hapanta prosdapanōsas], consuming everything like fire. So too the grammarians would have locustae named a locis ustis [from burnt places]. But, to say this in passing, to me [col. 474] locusta seems named from nothing other than locutio [speech], since it is as loquax [talkative] as the cicada, which they hold to be the symbol of talkativeness. Thus in the Pythagorist of Aristophon, in Athenaeus, book 6, a certain parasite boasts that he is λαλεῖν τέττιγα [lalein tettiga], a cicada in talkativeness. And Aelian, Historia book 6, ch. 19, calls τὸ τεττίγων φῦλον [to tettigōn phylon], the race of cicadas, λάλον [lalon], talkative. Hence Alexis in the Thraso, in Athenaeus, book 4:

— — — σοῦ δ' ἐγὼ λαλιστέραν Οὐ πώποτ' εἶδον, οὔτε κερκώπην, γύναι, Οὐ κίτταν, οὐκ ἀηδόνα, οὐ τρυγόνα, οὐ τέττιγα. [— — — sou d' egō lalisteran ou pōpot' eidon, oute kerkōpēn, gynai, ou kittan, ouk aēdona, ou trygona, ou tettiga.]

I, woman, have never seen anyone more talkative than you, not a cercops, not a magpie, not a nightingale, not a cicada. For Hesychius too Ἀχέτης [Achetēs] is ὁ ἄῤῥην τέττιξ ὁ λαλίστατος [ho arrhēn tettix ho lalistatos], the male cicada, most talkative. And, if we believe Servius, the long-lived Tithonus is fabled to have been turned into a cicada because old men are by nature more talkative. Finally, Tzetzes has much on the talkativeness of cicadas in book 10, History 301. This [III, 307] above all: that they are more talkative in the heat, and that their wings are pressed in vain to silence them, since they then chatter all the more. And therefore of talkative people the common proverb says, Τέττιγα δόξεις τῶν πτερῶν τάχα κεκρατηκέναι [Tettiga doxeis tōn pterōn tacha kekratēkenai], You will seem perhaps to have held a cicada by the wings. Now, that you may know the same is said of locusts, read these words of Theocritus, Idyll 5:
— — — Καὶ ἀκρίδες ὧδε λαλεῦνται, [— — — Kai akrides hōde laleuntai,]
Here too the locusts talk. And Meleager on the locust, Anthology book 3, ch. 24:
Ἐκκρέουσα φίλας ποσσὶ λάλους πτέρυγας, [Ekkreousa philas possi lalous pterygas,]

Striking with its feet its dear chattering wings: as though the locust spoke with its wings. But most to the point here is the verb κατακριδεύειν [katakrideuein], formed ἀπὸ τῶν ἀκρίδων [apo tōn akridōn], from locusts, which means to deafen someone with one's chatter, as if you were to say locustare [to locust]. Hesychius: Κατακριδεύσει· καταλήσει (read καταλαλήσει·) ἐπεὶ καὶ αἱ ἀκρίδες πολύφωνοί εἰσιν· [Katakrideusei; katalēsei (read katalalēsei;) epei kai hai akrides polyphōnoi eisin;] He will locust (if the word may be pardoned), he will overwhelm with chatter; for locusts are most loquacious. But, to return to the matter: when the Prophet says of the coming people of locusts, Before it fire shall consume, and behind it a flame shall burn, I think that in both places he is speaking of an extreme drought, which preceded and followed the arrival of the locusts. And therefore the Prophet says, Before it (the people of locusts) shall consume, etc. The land of Canaan is compared with the garden of Eden, as Egypt and the land of the Sodomites before the disaster sent by God, Gen 13:10. Before it, that is, before its arrival; as behind it, that is, after its departure; as in Zech 7:14. The land was desolate after them, that is, after their migration ^{R2}.
And nothing shall escape it.] That is, of the produce of the land. For they will consume everything so that absolutely nothing is left.

Verse 4. Its appearance is like the appearance of horses, and like horsemen so shall they run] As in Rev 9:7. And the shapes of the locusts were like horses prepared for battle. The Hebrews refer this to the speed of their running or flight, in which they are nearly equal to horses; we refer it in addition to the head or face, which is not unlike a horse's. From this the Italians call locusts cavallette. Hence Albertus, book 26: They have a head with the shape of a horse. And Aldrovandi [=Ulisse Aldrovandi, Ornithologia (1599–1603)]: They have a head somewhat like a horse's. And long before, Theodoret on Joel: Εἴ τις ἀκριβῶς κατίδοι τὴν κεφαλὴν τὴν ἀκρίδος, σφόδρα τῇ τοῦ ἵππου [III, 308] ἐοικυῖαν εὑρήσει· [Ei tis akribōs katidoi tēn kephalēn tēn akridos, sphodra tē tou hippou eoikuian heurēsei;] If anyone considers the head of a locust attentively, he will find it very similar to the head of a horse. And Muhammiaddin Assarhuriensis, a poet of some renown among the Arabs:

لها فخذ ابكر وساقا نعامة [lahā fakhdh abkur wa-sāqā naʿāma] وقادمتا نسر وجوجو ضيغم [wa-qādimatā nasr wa-jūjū ḍayghama] ☼ ذنبها افاعي الارض وانعمت عليها [dhanabuhā afāʿī al-arḍ wa-anʿamat ʿalayhā] [col. 475] جياد الخيل بالراس والغم [jiyād al-khayl bi-l-rās wa-l-ghamm] ☼

They have the thigh of camels, the legs of an ostrich, the wings of an eagle, the breast of a lion. Their tail is like that of the vipers of the earth; and the noble horses have graced them with their form in head and mouth. And another anonymous Arab in Damiri: في جرادة خلق عشرة من جبابرة الحيوان مع ضعفها وجه فرس وعينا فيل وعنق ثور وقرنا ايل وصدر اسد وبطن عقرب وجناحا نسر وفخذا جمل ورجالا نعامة وذنب حية [fī jarāda khalq ʿashara min jabābirat al-ḥayawān maʿa ḍaʿfihā wajh faras wa-ʿaynā fīl wa-ʿunuq thawr wa-qarnā ayyil wa-ṣadr asad wa-baṭn ʿaqrab wa-janāḥā nasr wa-fakhdhā jamal wa-rijlā naʿāma wa-dhanab ḥayya] In the locust, weak as it is, is the nature of ten great animals: 1. the face of a horse, 2. the eyes of an elephant, 3. the neck of a bull, 4. the horns of a stag, 5. the breast of a lion, 6. the belly of a scorpion, 7. the wings of an eagle, 8. the thighs of a camel, 9. the feet of an ostrich, 10. the tail of a serpent. In this list the face of a horse is put first of all. For بطن عقرب [baṭn ʿaqrab] the belly of a scorpion, read بطن عقاب [baṭn ʿuqāb] the belly of a black eagle. For the scorpion, which is smaller than the locust, can have no place among those great animals. True, there follows وجناحا نسر [wa-janāḥā nasr] and the wings of an eagle. But عقاب [ʿuqāb] and نسر [nasr] are different species of eagles. Abarbanel [=Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), commentary on the Bible] anxiously inquires why the Assyrians, whom he holds Joel to be treating here, are compared with horses or horsemen. At one moment he understands by horses the Centaurs, whom the horsemen of the Chaldeans resembled; at another he contends that their foot soldiers were like real horses in stature, strength and speed. Everyone sees how absurd this is. Of Centaurs there is here neither trace nor track; nor would any sane person believe that the Chaldeans are said by the Prophet to be like an animal that exists nowhere. And for foot soldiers to be compared with horsemen is novel and unheard of. Finally, who would say that the Assyrians were like horsemen, when they really were horsemen, and in great numbers? Scripture teaches this expressly in Ezek 23:6 12. 23. and XXVI, 7. 10. 11. Nahum. III, 2. Hab 1:8 etc.

Verse 5. Like the noise of chariots they will leap upon the tops of the mountains, like the noise of a flame of fire devouring stubble, like a strong people set in array for battle] This too fits locusts exactly, which fly with a great noise, [III, 309] fall upon the fields, and grind down the crops with their teeth. Hence John says of the locusts, Rev 9:9. The sound of their wings was as the sound of chariots, of many horses running to battle. Pliny, book 11, chapter 29: They fly with such a whirring of wings that they are taken for other birds. Remigius of Auxerre on Joel: They make a great sound when they are sent, so much so that their sound can be heard from the sixth milestone. Cyril: Φασὶ γὰρ οὐ δίχα κτύπου πράττεσθαι παρ᾽ αὐτῶν ἐν ἀγροῖς τὴν κατάπτωσιν· ἠχὼ δέ τινα τῶν ὀδόντων ἀποτελεῖσθαι βληχρὰν, περιθραυομένων αὐταῖς τῶν πεπτωκότων, ὡς ἀνέμου φλόγα διαῤῥιπίζοντος· [Phasi gar ou dicha ktypou prattesthai par᾽ autōn en agrois tēn kataptōsin; ēchō de tina tōn odontōn apoteleisthai blēchran, perithrauomenōn autais tōn peptōkotōn, hōs anemou phloga diarrhipizontos] They say that they do not fall upon the fields without noise; and that they also produce a faint sound with their teeth while they crush the fallen crops by chewing, like that of a wind fanning a flame ^{R3}. Moreover, a voice of their own is attributed to locusts. Thus in the Mirabilia the locust σκορπιομάχος [skorpiomachos] [col. 476], which fights the scorpion, κύκλῳ περιοῦσα τρύζει περὶ αὐτὸν [kyklō periousa tryzei peri auton], circling around it, chirps. And Aelian, book 6 of the History, ch. 19, describes βομβοῦσαν ἀκρίδα [bombousan akrida], καὶ πάρνοπα ὑποκράζοντα [kai parnopa hypokrazonta] (so I read instead of ὑποκρίζοντα [hypokrizonta] or ὑποκορίζοντα [hypokorizonta]), that is, the buzzing locust, and the parnops crying out softly. It must be admitted, however, that this voice is of uncertain origin. Pliny, in the place cited above: Their voice seems to come from the back of the head: in that place, at the joint of the shoulder blades, they are thought to have something like teeth, and by rubbing these together to produce a kind of whirring around the two equinoxes, as cicadas do around the solstice. But the same author says otherwise in ch. 51: It is indeed believed that locusts (make their sound) by the rubbing of their wings and thighs. So too the Philosopher, book 4 of the History, ch. 9: Τοῖς πηδαλίοις τρίβουσαι ποιοῦσι τὸν ψόφον [Tois pēdaliois tribousai poiousi ton psophon], They produce their noise by rubbing their hind legs. The poets attribute this voice, such as it is, to the wings. Mnesalchus, book 3 of the Anthology, ch. 24:
Οὐκ ἔτι δὴ πτερύγεσσι λιγυφθόγγοισιν ἀείσεις, Ἀκρὶ, κατ᾽ εὐκάρπους αὔλακας ἑζόμενα. [Ouk eti dē pterygessi ligyphthongoisin aeiseis, Akri, kat᾽ eukarpous aulakas hezomena.]
No longer will you sing with your sweet-sounding wings, O locust, sitting by the fruitful furrows. And again,
Ξουθᾶν ἐκ πτερύγων ἡδὺ κρέκουσα μέλος. [Xouthan ek pterygōn hēdy krekousa melos.]
Singing a sweet melody from your tawny wings. And in the same place Meleager:
Αὐτοφυὲς μίμημα λύρας, κρέκε μοί τι ποθεινὸν, Ἐκκρέουσα φίλας ποσσὶ λάλους πτέρυγας. [Autophyes mimēma lyras, kreke moi ti potheinon, Ekkreousa philas possi lalous pterygas.]
[III, 310] O you who by nature imitate the lyre, sing me something lovely, striking with your feet your dear vocal wings. And Phaennus:
Δαμοκρίτῳ μὲν ἐπὼ λιγυρὰν ὄκα Μοῦσαν ἐνίην Ἀκρὶς ἀπὸ πτερύγων, τὸν βαθὺν ὕπνον ἄγων. [Damokritō men epō ligyran oka Mousan eniēn Akris apo pterygōn, ton bathyn hypnon agōn.]

For Damocritus, when I, the locust, sent forth a sweet Muse from my wings, bringing on deep sleep. Nor should you be surprised that a voice in which there seems to be no elegance at all is praised. For the poets everywhere praise the locust, like the cicada, for its song. Leonidas:
Ἀκρίδι, τᾷ κατ᾽ ἄρουραν ἀηδόνι, καὶ δρυοκοίτᾳ Τέττιγι ξυνὸν τύμβον ἔτευξε Μυρώ. [Akridi, ta kat᾽ arouran aēdoni, kai dryokoita Tettigi xynon tymbon eteuxe Myrō.]
For the locust, the nightingale of the fields, and for the cicada that lies in the oaks, Myro made a common tomb. Anyte:
Οὐκ ἔτι λιγεία σε κατ᾽ ἀφνεὸν Ἄκιδος οἶκον, Ἀκρὶ, μελιζομέναν, ὄψεται ἠέλιος. [Ouk eti ligeia se kat᾽ aphneon Akidos oikon, Akri, melizomenan, opsetai ēelios.]

No longer, O tuneful locust, will the sun see you singing by the rich house of Acis. And much earlier Theocritus, Idyll 7, belittling himself (ἐξουθενίζων [exouthenizōn]) as unequal to a contest with a poet of great name:
— βάτραχος δὲ ποτ᾽ ἀκρίδας, ὥς τις ἐρίσδω· [— batrachos de pot᾽ akridas, hōs tis erisdō;]

Like a frog against locusts I compete. Nor was there any need to understand cicadas, whom he praises elsewhere for their song. For among locusts too there are some αἱ συρίζουσιν ἐναρμόνιον [hai syrizousin enarmonion], which produce a harmonious whistling, as the Scholiast says there. Accordingly in Idyll 5 Lacon invites Comatas to rest in the nearby wood for this reason:
Ψυχρὸν ὕδωρ τηνεὶ καταλείβεται· ὧδε πεφύκει Ποία, χᾀ στιβὰς ᾇδε, καὶ ἀκρίδες ὧδε λαλεῦντι. [Psychron hydōr tēnei kataleibetai; hōde pephykei Poia, cha stibas hade, kai akrides hōde laleunti.]
Cold water flows there; there grass has grown, and a couch, and locusts there chatter, or sing.

However that may be, the sacred writer passes from voice and sound to military order, and says in verse 5: It is like a strong people, set in array for battle. 6. Before its face the peoples shall tremble; all faces shall gather paleness. 7. They shall run like mighty soldiers; like men of war they shall climb the wall. Each shall march in his own ways, and they shall not break their paths. 8. And one shall not thrust another; each shall march in his own track. Even falling upon the sword they shall not be wounded. 9. They shall go through the city, they shall climb up into the houses, they shall enter in at the very windows like a thief.] In these words it must first be noted that this army, whatever it is, is now called not a people but like a people. So when the Prophet [col. 477] [III, 311] above ^{b)} called it a nation and a people, he was speaking metaphorically, calling a people those forces which are not really a people, but are like a people set in array for battle. Of the same kind is his addition that they run like mighty soldiers and climb the wall like men of war, so that no one should imagine real soldiers and warriors here. But although they are not soldiers, they are nevertheless rightly compared with real soldiers: 1. on account of their number and strength. It is like a strong people. Jerome: What is more innumerable and stronger than locusts, which human industry cannot resist? Cyril: Χρῆμα ἄμαχον, καὶ δυσκαταγώνιστον παντελῶς ἀνθρώποις, βρούχου καὶ ἀκρίδος ἐμβολή· [Chrēma amachon, kai dyskatagōniston pantelōs anthrōpois, brouchou kai akridos embolē] The onslaught of the bruchus and the locust is invincible, and utterly insuperable for men. Pisides describes their manner of fighting thus:

Τὸ πτηνὸν ὅπλον εἰς ἀνάμνησιν φόβου, [To ptēnon hoplon eis anamnēsin phobou,] Βέλος νεφῶδες ἐξ ἀδήλου τοξότου, [Belos nephōdes ex adēlou toxotou,] Λόγχην ἑτοίμην, αὐτοκίνητον δόρυ, [Lonchēn hetoimēn, autokinēton dory,] Πυκνὴν φάλαγγα, μυριόστομον ξίφος, [Pyknēn phalanga, myriostomon xiphos,] Πηδητικὴν ἔπαλξιν ἀστάτου μάχης. [Pēdētikēn epalxin astatou machēs.] Οὐχ ἵσταται γὰρ, ἀλλὰ πλήττει, καὶ τρέχει, [Ouch histatai gar, alla plēttei, kai trechei,] Ἕρπουσα πορθεῖ, καὶ κλονεῖ πτερουμένη. [Herpousa porthei, kai klonei pteroumenē.] Δοκεῖ δὲ φεύγειν, καὶ παλίνδρομος μένει. [Dokei de pheugein, kai palindromos menei.]

A flying weapon to arouse fear, a cloudy arrow (shot) by an unseen archer, a lance at the ready, a spear that moves of itself, a dense phalanx, a sword of a thousand battle-lines, a shifting bulwark of unstable combat. For it does not stand still, but strikes as it runs, lays waste as it creeps, and makes tumult as it flies. It seems to flee, and at once, running back, it stays. 2. They are compared with an army by reason of the order which they keep in flight and on the march. For they are like a strong people set in array for battle (in Hebrew ערוך, drawn up in order). Each will advance in his own ways, and they will not break their ranks, and one will not press upon another. Each will go in his own path. That this is so, Jerome asserts in these words: They fly in such order, by the disposition of God who commands them, that, like the little tesserae which are set in pavements by the hand of the craftsman, they keep their place and do not deviate toward another by so much as a point, so to speak, or a nail's breadth. Nor does he report this from uncertain tradition, but as an eyewitness, αὐτόπτης [autoptēs]. We saw this recently, he says, in this province (of Palestine). And Theodoret: Ἔστι γὰρ ἰδεῖν τὴν ἀκρίδα, τῶν πολεμίων δίκην, καὶ τειχῶν ἐπιβαίνουσαν, καὶ τοῖς ὁδοῖς βαδίζουσαν· καὶ οὐδ᾽ ὑπό τινος ἀνάγκης σκεδασθῆναι ἀνεχομένην, ἀλλ᾽ οἷον μετά τινος συμπνοίας ταύτην ἔφοδον ποιουμένην· [Esti gar idein tēn akrida, tōn polemiōn dikēn, kai teichōn epibainousan, kai tois hodois badizousan; kai oud᾽ hypo tinos anankēs skedasthēnai anechomenēn, all᾽ hoion meta tinos sympnoias tautēn ephodon poioumenēn;] For one may see locusts climb walls like enemies, and advance along the roads; and they do not suffer themselves to be torn apart by any force, but make their [III, 312] attack as if by a kind of mutual conspiracy. And Cyril: Φασὶ δὲ αὐτὰς στοιχηδὸν ἰέναι, καὶ ὡς ἐν τάξει διΐπτασθαι, καὶ ἥκιστα μὲν ἀπονοσφίζεσθαι, περιέπειν δὲ οὕτως ἀλλήλας, ὡσανεὶ καὶ ἀδελφαὶ, φύσεως αὐτῆς [Phasi de autas stoichēdon ienai, kai hōs en taxei diiptasthai, kai hēkista men aponosphizesthai, periepein de houtōs allēlas, hōsanei kai adelphai, physeōs autēs] (read αὐταῖς [autais]) βραβευούσης τὸ φιλάλληλον [brabeuousēs to philallēlon]. They say that they go in order, and fly as if in battle-lines, and are very little separated, and follow one another like sisters, nature dispensing mutual love to them. We have already shown above ^{c)} that the Arabs too, in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], teach the same. They gather, they say, كالعسكر [ka-l-ʿaskar] like an army. For when the first of them migrates, all follow and migrate together. And when the first halts, all the rest halt. But most relevant here is that from the Arabic verb نظم [naẓama] nadama, which means to join in a fixed series and to string together, as pearls in a necklace, a swarm of locusts is called منظوم [manẓūm] mandoum. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: المنظوم الجماعة من الجراد [al-manẓūm al-jamāʿa min al-jarād] Almandoum, a swarm of locusts. Accordingly Sigebert, on the multitude of locusts which ravaged Gaul in the year 874: What is wonderful to tell, it flew in such order, with leaders sent ahead to mark out the camp the day before, that military discipline could be seen in these animals. 3. Like soldiers the locusts scale the walls, [col. 478] march through the city, run upon the wall, climb up into the houses, enter through the windows]. As Moses ^{d)} says to Pharaoh concerning the Egyptian locusts: They shall fill your houses, and the houses of all your servants, and the houses of all the Egyptians. Hence Jerome on Joel: Nothing is impassable to locusts, since they penetrate fields, crops, trees, cities, houses, and the privacy of bedchambers. And Cyril: Οἴκοις αὐτοῖς καὶ πόλεσιν εἰσπεφοιτηκότα, καὶ παρενοχλοῦντα δεινῶς, τὸν ἐκ τῶν ἀκρίδων ἕξουσι στρατόν· [Oikois autois kai polesin eispephoitēkota, kai parenochlounta deinōs, ton ek tōn akridōn hexousi straton;] They will endure an army of locusts that enters their very houses and cities and troubles them dreadfully. Lest this seem incredible, here is an eyewitness beyond all objection, Theodoret, I mean, on this passage! Οὐκ ἀπόχρη τῶν περιβόλων τὸ ὕψος ἐμποδὼν τῇ τούτων εἰσόδῳ γενέσθαι. Ἀλλὰ ῥαδίως μὲν ὑπερβήσονται τὰ τείχη· κλέπταις δὲ παραπλησίως διὰ θυρίδων εἰς τὰς οἰκίας εἰσελεύσονται. Καὶ τοῦτο δὲ οὐ μόνον ὑπὸ πολεμίων, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑπὸ ἀκρίδων γεγενημένων [Ouk apochrē tōn peribolōn to hypsos empodōn tē toutōn eisodō genesthai. Alla rhadiōs men hyperbēsontai ta teichē; kleptais de paraplēsiōs dia thyridōn eis tas oikias eiseleusontai. Kai touto de ou monon hypo polemiōn, alla kai hypo akridōn gegenēmenōn] (read γεγενήμενον [gegenēmenon]) πολλάκις ἐθεασάμεθα. οὐ πετόμεναι γὰρ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ κατὰ τῶν τειχῶν ἀνερποῦσαι, διὰ τῶν φωταγώγων εἰς τοὺς οἴκους εἰσίασι. [pollakis etheasametha. ou petomenai gar monon, alla kai kata tōn teichōn anerpousai, dia tōn phōtagōgōn eis tous oikous eisiasi.] The height of the walls is not enough to prevent their (the enemies') entry. For they will easily climb over the walls, and, like thieves, will enter the houses through the windows. This we have often seen done not only by enemies but also by locusts. For not only by flying, but also by creeping up the walls, they penetrate into houses through the windows. And Pliny had already noted that locusts also come to houses and gnaw everything with their bite, even the doors of buildings. So Hieronymus Mercurialis [III, 313] gives as a sign of the plague of Venice and Padua that many bruchi had appeared along the streets and walls. And so in the histories of the Arabs I find that locusts sometimes fall onto their tables. Thus in Tabrani, Algesen, son of Ali, says: We were sitting at table and feasting, I and my brother Muhammed, son of Alchanaphia, and the sons of my paternal uncle, Abdalla, and Kethem, and Alphadal, sons of Alibas, فوقعت الجرادة على المايدة [fa-waqaʿat al-jarāda ʿalā al-māyida] and a locust fell upon the table, etc. Damir collected more of this kind, from which it is plain that they penetrate into the houses of the Arabs. 4. They rush through missiles (or through swords) and are not wounded.] For other animals flee at the sight of a man, but these attack a man of their own accord. Accordingly, when a cloud of locusts comes on, everyone hides in the houses, lest by going out they provoke them. Democritus in the Geoponica, book 13: Ἐὰν νέφος ἀκρίδων ἐπέρχηται, πάντες ἔνδον μενέτωσαν ἀφανεῖς, καὶ παρελεύσονται τὸ χωρίον [Ean nephos akridōn eperchētai, pantes endon menetōsan aphaneis, kai pareleusontai to chōrion]. Nor is there reason to hope that they can be driven off by brandished weapons. For they are carried along with a blind rush, and neither fear swords nor are easily wounded by them. By their lightness, namely, and the slenderness of their little bodies, they elude any blows. Moreover, as Claudian rightly observed,
— — a covering grown with it hardens on the back; nature has armed the skin. — —

Hence John Rev 9:9: And they had breastplates, as it were breastplates of iron. They will not be wounded.] In Hebrew לא יבצעו, for לא יפצעו. So here again Beth stands for Pe, as above in עבשר. The ancients render it very differently. But this version is most fitting ^{R4}.

[III, 314] 5. They will march through the city.] In Hebrew בעיר ישקו, a verb derived from the noun שוק, that is, leg; as in Es. XXXIII, 4: כמשק גבים שוקק בו, as with the march of locusts he marches against it, namely the enemy against the Assyrian; that is, he marches in such a way that he cannot be turned back. For whatever you do, locusts press on, and they do not withdraw until they are sated. This coheres with what precedes, at the beginning of the same verse, which we touched on above: Your spoil is gathered as the bruchus gathers; that is, "The enemy will strip you as the bruchus strips a field, which it leaves only when it is bare." 6. Rightly, then, this enemy, however small, is terrible to men. Accordingly the Prophet had said in verse 6: Before its face the peoples will tremble; all faces will gather paleness. And in Ier. LI, 27, ילק סמר is perhaps a dreadful bruchus, as in Hesychius βρέττανα φοβερὰ [brettana phobera], a terrible locust.

Verse 10: Before it the earth is shaken, the heavens are moved; the sun and moon are darkened, [col. 479] and the stars withdraw their brightness.] Some understand earthquakes, thunder and eclipses. But Jerome holds that this is said hyperbolically: Not that the force of locusts is so great that they can move the heavens and shake the earth, but that to those suffering adversity, from the greatness of their terror, the sky seems to fall and the earth to heave. Yet the same author explains what is said at the end of the verse about the sun, moon and stars as meant literally: Because of the multitude of locusts covering the sky, the sun and moon will be turned into darkness, and the stars will withdraw their light, while the cloud of locusts set in between does not let the light reach the earth. So too Remigius on this passage: By their density and multitude they are wont to fill (read drive back) the rays of the sun from the earth, and to overshadow it like clouds. Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] writes that this happened in Egypt, Exod 10:15: וחפא ית עין שמשא דארעא וחשיכת ארעא, And it (the mass of locusts) covered the eye of the sun of the land, and the land was darkened. So Pliny writes that locusts overshadow the sun. And the Historia Saracenica, p. 98, says that in the year (of the Hijra) 317 there was so great a multitude of locusts in Egypt انه منع شعاع الشمس ان تقع علي الارض [annahu manaʿa shuʿāʿ al-shams an taqaʿa ʿalā al-arḍ] that it kept the rays of the sun from reaching the earth. Likewise Eutychius, vol. 2, p. 518: ووقع بمصر من الجراد ما لا يوصف كثرته حتي منع شعاع الشمس ان تقع علي الارض [wa-waqaʿa bi-Miṣr min al-jarād mā lā yūṣafu kathratuhu ḥattā manaʿa shuʿāʿ al-shams an taqaʿa ʿalā al-arḍ] And there fell upon Egypt a countless multitude of locusts, so that it prevented the rays of the sun from reaching the earth. And Cadamosto [=Alvise Cadamosto, Navigazioni (1455-56)], [III, 315] ch. 13 of the Navigations, on the deserts near the Nigritae: In the same regions we also saw a countless multitude of locusts shading the air; for they come almost every three years and darken the sky. And a little later: And they are so numerous that they shade the sky over a space of twelve miles. And Thuanus, book 84, on locusts in Syria: Flying like a dense cloud, the day being darkened at full noon, they grazed the fields all around. Hence Marcellus Palingenius in the Zodiacus, book 8:
— — — — and grim locusts veil the shining sun like a mist.

And we have shown ^{e)} that the two Hebrew names of locusts חגב and צלצל refer to this: the latter taken from shadow, the former from the veil that it spreads before the sun. Indeed, for this very reason Joel says that before them the heavens are moved, that is, the powers of the heavens, as in Matt 24:29. For since the chief power of the heaven lies in the light with which it shines upon us, why, when that light is blocked and, so to speak, extinguished, should not the power of heaven, and thus the heaven itself, be said to be moved? The earth, moreover, is said to be moved when men, the inhabitants of the earth, are shaken by grave fear or by sudden and unforeseen calamity. Examples of this expression abound everywhere in the Scriptures. If anyone objects that the Prophet's words, The sun and moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their brightness, cannot refer to locusts, which in flight darken the sun but never the moon and stars, since they fly only by day, I shall reply with Pliny that the ancient writers reported that they do not fly by night because of the cold, not knowing that they cross even distant seas, with continuous hunger for many days.

Oseas XIII, 3., to show how vain is the glory of those who think themselves safe under the protection of the idols they worship. They shall be, he says, as the morning cloud, [col. 480] and as the dew that passes away early, as the chaff that is driven by the whirlwind out of the threshing floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney.] The chimney there is ארבה arubba, for which the Greeks read ארבה arbe, that is, locust; for these two words, though they differ greatly in their vowel points, nevertheless have the same letters. Hence arose the Greek version ὡς ἀτμὶς ἀπὸ ἀκρίδων [hōs atmis apo akridōn], as vapour from locusts. And a most learned and most pious man understands a mist consisting of locusts, which obscures the light of the sun but, passing quickly, soon vanishes and restores the sunlight that it had, as it were, intercepted for a short time. Jerome understands the very breath of the locusts, saying that Ephraim is compared to ἀτμῷ [atmō], that is, to vapour, or to the breath and air which comes out of the mouth of the locust so thinly that it is not perceived. Theodoret says that the wicked are to be destroyed just as ἀτμὸν, ἐν ἀέρι γινόμενον, νέφος ἀκρίδων ἐπιγινόμενον διαλύει [atmon, en aeri ginomenon, nephos akridōn epiginomenon dialyei], a cloud [III, 316] of locusts, falling upon it, dissolves a vapour raised in the air. But what the Greeks thought matters little, since the Hebrew text has something else, namely smoke from the chimney, ἀπὸ καπνοδόχης [apo kapnodochēs], as Theodotion rightly rendered it. And Cyril follows this. Seneca too uses the comparison of smoke and cloud on a similar theme, Troades, Act 2.
— — as dark smoke from hot fires vanishes within a brief space; as the onset of Arctic Boreas scatters the heavy clouds we saw just now: so this spirit by which we are ruled flows away.

Verse 11. And the Lord uttered his voice before his army, that his camp may be very great, that he may be strong who executes his word. For the day of the Lord is great and very terrible: and who can abide it?] That is, "The Lord by his word has enlisted great forces, to execute upon sinners a heavy judgment which no one can withstand." This seems to be the Prophet's meaning, although the interpreters think very differently. And here the threats end. They are followed by exhortations to repentance and by many promises in God's name. Among these, since they concern the locusts, we shall also explain what is found in the twentieth and twenty-fifth verses.

Verse 20. And I will remove the northern one far from you, and drive him into a thirsty and desolate land: his face toward the eastern sea, and his rear toward the hinder sea. And his stench shall go up, his foulness, I say, shall go up; because he has done great things.] Those who refer these things to the Chaldaeans press this passage above all, holding that by the northern one the Assyrians are meant, who had come from the north. Jerome: He inserted the north, so that we should understand not the real locust, which usually comes from the south, but under the figure of the locust the Assyrians and Chaldaeans. Abarbanel understands not only the Assyrians, who carried off the ten tribes, and the Babylonians, by whom the first temple was destroyed, but also the Romans, who destroyed the second. For all of these live to the north of Judaea, yet in such a way that the Assyrians and Babylonians lie toward the east and the Romans toward the west. And accordingly he holds that the Prophet placed some of these northerners at the face and others at the rear, since for the Hebrews the east is regarded as the face of the world and the west as its hinder part. But it is plain that this too pertains to the locusts by which Judaea was to be laid waste. With respect, namely, to Jerusalem, the city in which Joel seems to have prophesied, these locusts were either to the north, or to the east, or to the west. He does not mention southern ones because, since Jerusalem lay almost at the far south of the land of Canaan, the southern ones were few in relation to the city and were included under the others. With this premised, [III, 317] the words of the Prophet will contain nothing to detain the reader. The northern one, he says (that is, the part of the army of locusts which is to the north of the city), I will remove far from you, and drive it into a dry and desolate land, that is, into the deserts of Arabia. Its face toward the eastern sea, that is, [col. 481] the part turned toward the face of the world (or toward the east), into the Dead Sea, situated to the east of the city; and its rear toward the hinder sea, that is, the western part of the army into the western, or Mediterranean, sea. And its stench shall go up, its foulness (I say) shall go up. Its stench and its foulness are in Hebrew באשו and צחנהו; of these the latter occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew text, but is used by the Chaldee paraphrast at Ezek 23:20. For the Syrians too ܨܚܢܐ [צחנא] is the very same thing, with the guttural elided. Why then do the Greek translators here have Ἀναβήσεται ὁ βρόμος αὐτοῦ [Anabēsetai ho bromos autou], His noise shall go up? Hence Cyril: Ἐκεῖ τὸν βροῦχον καὶ τὴν ἀκρίδα διολέσαι φησι, δυσαχθῆ δὲ γενέσθαι τὸν βρόμον αὐτῶν [Ekei ton brouchon kai tēn akrida diolesai phēsi, dysachthē de genesthai ton bromon autōn]; There (in the Mediterranean sea) he says the bruchus and the locust perished, but their noise was grievous. I say that in both places there is a corruption, and that instead of βρόμον [bromon] one should read βρῶμον [brōmon], as Theodoret quite rightly has ^{R5}. For βρῶμος [brōmos] is stench, whence βρωμώδης [brōmōdēs], for fetid and rank, occurs frequently in Dioscorides and Athenaeus. But nothing is more frequent than this corruption. So also in Hesychius βρόμος [bromos] is rendered ὀσμὴ [osmē]. And in Dioscorides, book 5, sea water kept for a long time at length becomes ἄβρομος [abromos], that is, loses its rankness. And in Athenaeus, book 3, chapter 33: Τάριχος τέλειος, καὶ μὴ βρομώδης [Tarichos teleios, kai mē bromōdēs]; Salted fish perfectly cured, and not rank. That this is the very same as the Hebrew צחנה you may gather also from the fact that the Talmudists call small salted fish צחנתא, and the Arabs صحناة [ṣaḥnāh], namely from their rank smell. This, then, is what Joel says: that the locusts, plunged into the sea, would give off a foul and rank odour. Moreover, that they are often carried off by the wind from the lands they devastate and plunged into the seas, we have shown ^{f)} from Pliny, Jerome and Orosius, on the words of Moses Exod 10:19: God sent a west wind which, bringing the locusts, cast them into the Red Sea. As to what is added about the foul odour, it is proved by these words of Jerome about the locusts whose swarms, he writes, covered Judaea in his own time: When the wind rose, they were cast headlong into the first and the last sea, etc. And when the shores of both seas were filled with heaps of dead locusts which the waters had vomited up, [III, 318] their putrefaction and stench were so noxious that it even corrupted the air, and a pestilence arose among beasts as well as men. And so too what Augustine ^{g)}, Orosius ^{h)}, Freculphus ^{i)}, etc. relate, after Julius Obsequens and other older writers: that in the consulship of M. Plautius and M. Fulvius Flaccus, when the winds had cast an immense multitude of locusts into the African sea and the waves had driven them onto the shores, their wasting and putrefied mass gave off so pestilential a vapour that in Numidia alone eight hundred thousand people are reported to have perished, and on the coast around Carthage and Utica more than two hundred thousand; and at Utica itself thirty thousand soldiers, who had been stationed there to garrison all Africa, were destroyed and wiped out. Sigebert too, in the place cited above, relates that a multitude of locusts which had devastated Gaul, carried off by the blast of the winds and drowned in the British sea, was thrown back onto the shore by the backwash of the Ocean, and from its stench produced a corruption of the air, from which arose a great famine and a pestilence that carried off a third of mankind. More of this kind could be adduced, were these not more than sufficient ^{R6}.

Verse 25: And I will restore to you the years that the arbe, jelek, chasil and gazam have eaten, my great army, which I sent among you.] In verses 22, 23 and 24 the Prophet, in God's name, promises the exact opposite of all the threats that had gone before: namely, that the pastures of the wilderness will grow green, the trees will bear their fruit, and the fig tree and the vine will yield their strength, since God will send down abundant rain, both early and late, at the proper time; and the threshing floors will be filled with grain, and the vats of the winepresses will overflow with new wine and oil. Thus the years will be restored [col. 482] to the wretched Jews, that is, the yearly produce which the four kinds of locusts had consumed: not one kind in each year, as we have pointed out, but all at the same time, succeeding one another. For how many years this plague afflicted Canaan we simply do not know. We know only that the Jews were afflicted by these locusts both severely and for several years, God thus punishing the stubborn and those who despised his name. That is why he calls the locusts his great army. So do the Arabs as well. Thus in Damir a law is cited as enacted and promulgated by Muhammad: لا تقتلوا الجراد فانها جند [III, 319] الله الاعظم [lā taqtulū al-jarād fa-innahā jund Allāh al-aʿẓam] You shall not kill locusts, for they are the army of the most great God. Not to mention the tale told by Ibn-Omar, that locusts fell into the hands of that same pseudo-Prophet with this inscription on their wings: نحن جند الله الاكبر [naḥnu jund Allāh al-akbar] We are the army of the most great God.

Those who twist into a mystical sense what has so far been adduced from Joel about the locusts make a great show of objecting that nothing is found in the histories of Kings and Chronicles about so severe an invasion of locusts into Judaea, or about the famine that followed it. Jerome: For neither the history of Kings nor of Chronicles relates it; and certainly, had it happened, Scripture would never have been silent, just as we read of the famine of three years and six months under Elias. Abarbanel on Joel, Question 4: If the famine and the locusts were so severe, whether in the days of Joram, son of Ahab, and in the days of Elisha, or in the time of Manasseh, when, according to the Seder Olam, Joel, Nahum and Habakkuk are said to have prophesied, the question is why no mention of this is made in the books of Kings. Or, if that very point is disputed, why did Jeremiah not mention it, who reports many things of no great importance? But neither in the books of Chronicles, where things are narrated more fully, does a single word about this occur, which is very remarkable. I reply that the sacred writers did not set themselves the task of reporting how often God afflicted Judaea with famine. Indeed, if the whole of Scripture is gone through from beginning to end, it will be found that the history of a famine is nowhere recounted except in passing, as an appendix, so to speak, to some other narrative. Thus in Gen 12:10 and XXVI, 1. a severe famine in the land of Canaan is reported under Abraham and Isaac, so that we might know why the former went to Egypt and the latter to Palestine [Philistia, Gen 26:1]. And in the forty-first chapter of Genesis Moses describes the seven-year famine that Joseph had foretold in order to pave the way for the marvellous histories of Joseph and his brothers, and of the harsh servitude of the Israelites in Egypt, from which God delivered them with a strong hand and an outstretched arm. In the whole book of Judges there is no history of a famine. Yet at the beginning of the book of Ruth it is told that Elimelech, a Bethlehemite, withdrew to the land of Moab on account of a famine that raged in Judaea under the judges. Likewise, because it concerned us to know how, once the family of Saul had been cut off, the kingdom of David was established, the second book of Samuel, chapter 21, deals with a three-year famine that could not be stopped except by crucifying seven men of Saul's line. Again, the histories of famine under the prophets Elias and Elisha, 1 Reg. XVIII, 2. and 2 Reg. IV, 38. and VIII, 1., are reported because of the miracles they performed on that account. Finally, Luke touches on the famine that occurred under Claudius in a single brief word, only to show that it had been foretold by Agabus, and that it gave the Christians of Antioch occasion to send alms [III, 320] to their brethren in Jerusalem. Apart from those cited, no other history of a famine is to be found in either Testament. Therefore, since in a history of four thousand years so little is reported on this subject, and that only in passing and for the sake of something else, why should [col. 483] we be surprised that the history of the famine which Joel had foretold has been passed over?

notes.text: There are, however, interpreters who take the word שחר in the sense of darkness, with which the dense swarms of locusts obscure the sun. So Abu-Walid, cited by Pococke [=Edward Pococke (1604–1691), orientalist; commentaries on Micah, Malachi, Hosea and Joel] p. 116: שבה אנתשאר אלגראר פי אלבלאד באנתשאר אלצו פי אלגו הדא קול גירנא וחשביהם באנתשאר אלטלאם אולא, the spreading of the locusts over the region is compared to the spreading of light in the air. This is what others say. But the comparison with the spreading of darkness is more fitting, as is said in Exod 10:15: They covered the face of the whole earth, so that the earth was [III, 306] darkened. But R. Tanchum, Pococke adds, who no doubt had seen him and weighed his opinion, thinks otherwise. For after saying that he compares אנתשאר אלגראד באנתשאר אלצו אנר אלצבאה, the spreading of the locusts with the spreading of the light of the dawn, he adds: וקיל אן שחר הנא אלטלאם משתק מן שחור אי אנה יחגב אלצו לכתרתה פיציר אלטלאם מבסוטא עלי אלגבאל כמא קאל, and it is said (by some) that שחר here is darkness, derived from שחור, to be black, because by their multitude they block or veil the light, so that darkness is thereby spread over the mountains, according to what he said before, a day of darkness and gloom, which agrees with what we find in Exod 10:15: They covered the surface of the whole earth. But he says: אלאול אטהר ואנסב, the former opinion is clearer and more fitting. — C. G. Justi, in his notes on this passage, holds that the noun שחר is to be taken in the sense of twilight, because the notion of something joyful is attached to the dawn, which in no way suits this passage. — Francisco Alvarez writes in his Accounts of Journeys Made through Ethiopia that swarms of locusts shine in the sky with the yellow colour of their wings, and that from this shining the Ethiopians recognize their approach before they arrive; and it is Oedmann's [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde] opinion, in den Vermischten Sammlungen, fasc. 6, ch. 8, p. 75, that the words of Joel allude to the same thing.
notes.label: R1

notes.text: Oedmann, fasc. 6, ch. 8, p. 77, relates the words behind them a flame will burn to the fact that places laid waste by locusts truly look as if scorched by fire, as Mariti reports in his Account of a Journey Made through the Island of Cyprus, vol. 1, p. 258, since locusts consume not only crops and grasses but also the roots.
notes.label: R2

notes.text: The locusts passing over our heads roared with the sound of a great cataract, says Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)] in Descript. Animall. p. 81. A learned Maronite affirmed the very same to Norberg; his account may be read in Norberg's ninth letter in vol. 6, part 2 of Björnståhl's collection of letters (Biörnstähls Briefe auf seinen ausländischen Reisen, Sechsten Bandes Zweytes Heft), pp. 364–365.
notes.label: R3

notes.text: The Alexandrinus: καὶ ἐν τοις βελεσιν αὐτοι πεσενται, καὶ ου μη συντελεσθωσι [kai en tois belesin autoi pesentai, kai ou mē syntelesthōsi]. The Vulgate translator: and they will fall through the windows, and will not be destroyed. The Syriac: ܛܠ ܡܣܘܢܝܗܘܢ ܢܦܠܘܢ ܘܠܐ ܢܫܠܡܘܢ ܨܒܘ ܠܥܝܢܐ [טל מסוניהון נפלון ולא נשלמון צבו לעינא], they will fall under the weight of their arms, and will not bring the matter to an end. The Chaldee: גבר בכבישיה אזלין לאתר דאנין שליחין קטלין ולא מקבלין ממון, each goes along his path to the place to which they are sent; they slaughter, and do not accept money. “It is evident,” says Pococke p. 144, “that the root בצע has various meanings. 1. It denotes to make gain, or to be greedy for profit or gain, as in Proverb. XV, 27, בוצע בצע, one who is given to gain, and Hab 2:9, בוצע בצע רע, greedy of evil gain, and often elsewhere; and in this sense the Chaldee uses it here. An Arabic manuscript translated it from the Hebrew thus: ورا السلاح يقعون ولا يطمعون [wa-rā al-silāḥ yaqaʿūna wa-lā yaṭmaʿūna], they will fall behind the sword, and will not make gain. 2. To complete, or to bring to an end, as in Esaj. X, 12, כי יבצע יהוה את כל מעשהו, when the Lord has completed all his work, and Lament. II, 17, בצע אמרתו, he has fulfilled his word. In this sense the Greek, the printed Arabic [in the Polyglots], and the Syriac took it. 3. To cut down, cut off, wound, as in Job 6:9, ויבצעני, and that he would cut me down, and Esaj. XXXVIII, 12, ויבצעני, he will cut me off, and Amos 9:1, ובצעם, and strike them (or wound them, as in the margin); and thus it agrees with פצע (ב and פ being interchanged), which de- [III, 314] notes to wound. This meaning R. Tanchum also confirms from the Arabic language, in which بضع [baḍaʿa] means to cut up, to split, or to break into pieces, as also in Chaldee. Therefore both in him and in Abu Walid we read here لا ينجرحون [lā yanjariḥūna], they will not be wounded.”
notes.label: R4

notes.text: That certain ancient copies once had Βρωμον [Brōmon] is clear also from the Arabic version in the Polyglots, which was translated from the Alexandrian Greek, since it has: ويصعد نتنه وترتفع رايحته [wa-yaṣʿadu natnuhu wa-tartafiʿu rāyiḥatuhu], and its stench will go up, and its smell will rise.
notes.label: R5

notes.text: Whoever wants more from the travel accounts of more recent writers should consult OEDMANN, Fasc. 3, Chapter 10, p. 87, and Fasc. 6, Chapter 8, p. 78.
